To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have solved the three-dimensional structure of Ebola virus nucleoproteins at 5.6 Å resolution, and identified a new mechanism for Ebola virus nucleoprotiens to self-assemble and form the nucleocapsid.

we have determined the structure of the Ebola virus NP nucleocapsid-like assembly at 8 Å resolution using electron cryomicroscopy and identified new regulatory elements in the NP that impact viral RNA synthesis.

we have solved the structure of Ebola virus nucleoproteins in a nucleocapsid-like state at 5.7 Å resolution using cryo-EM, and that this structure reveals a new regulatory role of the nucleoprotein in viral RNA synthesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms of Ebola virus (EBOV) nucleocapsid-like assembly.
understanding the molecular mechanism of Ebola Virus nucleocapsid-like assembly, a process that is essential for viral replication and is required for the development of new antiviral drugs.
the structure and function of Ebola virus nucleoproteins and how the structure and function is regulated.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the authors have used a novel hybrid approach to generate a high-resolution structure of Ebola virus Nucleoprotein (NP) and to identify novel regulatory elements.
the authors have determined the 3D structure of eNP and that this structure is consistent with the known structure of the eNPs from other studies.
the N termini and helices α22–α23 of the nucleoprotein of Ebola virus are context-dependent regulatory modules that regulate viral RNA synthesis and are required for viral replication.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identified a novel regulatory role for a region of eNP, which we call CDRM, and we showed that this region is important for NC assembly and viral transcription and replication.
we identified a novel mechanism of nucleocapsid assembly for the Ebola virus, and this mechanism may be conserved among other viruses.

the N-terminal domain of Ebola virus nucleoproteins is important for nucleocapsid assembly and that this domain can act as a context-dependent regulatory module (CDRM) to modulate viral RNA synthesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the N termini of eNP and the α22-α22-α23 region of eNP function in a context-dependent manner to promote or inhibit the assembly of the viral nucleocapids.
we identified a novel mechanism for nucleocapsid-like assembly and identified a new therapeutic target.
Ebola virus nucleoproteins assemble into higher-ordered nucleocapsid-like structures that serve as the scaffold upon which the virus replicates its genome.
